text.p: French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin formed a left-wing cabinet on Tuesday, including Communists and Greens, to carry out election campaign pledges to tackle record unemployment.
Socialist Martine Aubry, 46, was named as number two in charge of a superministry for employment and social security in the Socialist-dominated "Pink-Green-Red" cabinet.

The cabinet comprises 14 full ministers, five of them women, two ministers delegate and 10 secretaries of state after the left beat Chirac's right-wing allies in Sunday's stunning parliamentary election upset.

Aubry, daughter of former European Commission president Jacques Delors, is a sharp-minded former labour minister. The appointments were read out by Dominiques de Villepin, secretary general of conservative President Jacques Chirac's office.
Foreign minister Hubert Vedrine, 49, is a leading expert on strategy and international relations who served as an aide to late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.

Vedrine has criticised Chirac's moves to bring France back into NATO's U.S.-led military wing, saying Paris should not make concessions without achieving a real shift of power to the Europeans within the Atlantic Alliance.
Serving under him with the European affairs portfolio will be minister delegate Pierre Moscovici of the Socialist Party.

New finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn drafted the Socialist party's economic policy which includes pledges to create 700,000 youth jobs and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss of pay.

Strauss-Kahn will have to balance aims of pushing through the reforms with no tax hikes, all the while meeting another pledge of joining a single European Union currency from 1999 without imposing further austerity.
Defence minister Alain Richard, 51, is a little-known parliamentary expert in state budgeting, with no apparent experience in defence affairs.
A first cabinet meeting will be held on Thursday at 10 a.m. (0800 GMT).

The government includes Communists for the first time since 1984 in a comeback after the Cold War, but consigned to ministries where they would have little leverage to impose views opposed to European integration.
Jospin needed the Communists to secure a majority in the 577-member parliament.
Communist Jean-Claude Gayssot, best known for co-authoring a tough anti-racism law, becomes transport minister while party comrade Marie-George Buffet, 48, was named minister of youth and sports.
Dominique Voynet, the iron lady of the Greens, was named environment minister.
Socialist Elisabeth Guigou was appointed justice minister, and Jospin's close adviser Claude Allegre, a university professor, minister of education, research and technology.
Segolene Royal, 44, was named minister delegate on school education.
The premier's other closest political associate, Daniel Vaillant, was named Minister for Relations with Parliament.
Jean-Pierre Chevenement, leader of the Citizens' Movement that opposes the Maastricht Treaty on European Union and a single currency, was named Interior Minister.
Strasbourg mayor Catherine Trautmann will be minister of culture and communications, and government spokeswoman. Another Socialist, Louis Le Pensec, takes charge of agriculture and fisheries.
Centre-left Radical Socialist Party, Emile Zuccarelli will be minister of the civil service, administrative reform and decentralisation.
A founder of the Medecins Sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders) medical charity, Bernard Kouchner was named secretary of state for health.

The Socialists and their close allies won 273 seats in the 577-member Assembly, the Communists 38 and the Greens seven. The Greens claim eight deputies, saying one of the Socialists is allied with their party.
